data.title: Talk to your data
data.subtitle: Pick a dataset, look at the chart or table, then judge each AI claim. Is the AI right or wrong about the numbers?

datasets.label: ☕ Café sales (2025)
datasets.info: Chai Corner's monthly sales. Revenue is in rupees.

judgments.question: Which month had the highest revenue?
judgments.truth: Dec: Rs 1,850,000. The AI is right.

judgments.question: What was the average monthly revenue?
judgments.truth: The average is Rs 1,344,583. The AI gave the median (the middle value), not the average. A mixed-up measure.

judgments.question: What will revenue be in January 2026?
judgments.ai_claim: January 2026 revenue will be exactly Rs 1,950,000, continuing the upward trend.
judgments.truth: Nobody can know exactly. Revenue did rise from September to December, but last January (Rs 1,260,000) was far lower than December (Rs 1,850,000), so there may be a seasonal dip. A sensible prediction gives a range and states its assumptions. An exact number is false confidence.

datasets.label: 🎓 Grade 10 maths results
datasets.info: 16 students, anonymised. Homework is the % of homework completed; Score is the final test out of 100.

judgments.question: Which class scored higher on average?
judgments.ai_claim: Class A, averaging 65 compared with 58.75 for Class B.
judgments.truth: Class A: 65, Class B: 58.75. The AI is right.

judgments.question: How many students scored below 50?
judgments.truth: 5 students: S03, S07, S10, S12, S14. The AI miscounted. Counting is surprisingly easy for AI to get wrong.

judgments.question: Does doing more homework lead to higher scores?
judgments.ai_claim: Yes. Doing more homework causes higher scores, so making homework compulsory will raise results.
judgments.truth: There's a very strong link (correlation 0.98), but that doesn't prove homework causes the scores. Motivated students may do both. And 16 students is a small sample. Correlation isn't causation.

datasets.label: 🏥 Clinic appointments (one week)
datasets.info: A small clinic's bookings for one week. Wait is the average wait in minutes.

judgments.question: Which day has the most no-shows?
judgments.truth: Mon, with 11. The AI is right.

judgments.question: What's the no-show rate for the week?
judgments.ai_claim: The no-show rate is about 7 per day, or 7%.
judgments.truth: 43 no-shows out of 302 bookings = 14.2%. The AI confused an average count per day with a rate.

judgments.question: Why are Monday waits so long?
judgments.ai_claim: Monday waits are long because of staff shortages at the start of the week.
judgments.truth: The data shows Monday has the most bookings (62) and the longest wait (48 minutes). It says nothing about staff. The AI invented a cause. More bookings is one likely factor worth investigating.

data.question: ChatGPT writes fluent emails, essays and code. How do you think it learned to do that?

options.label: Programmers wrote grammar rules for it
options.feedback: Not quite. Nobody wrote grammar rules for it. Language is far too messy for rules to capture.

options.label: It read huge amounts of text and learned the patterns
It looks up every answer on the internet
options.feedback: Not quite. Some assistants can search the web as an extra tool, but the model itself doesn't look things up.

options.label: I'm not sure
options.feedback: That's fine. That's what this lesson is for.

data.explanation: It was trained on enormous amounts of text and learned the patterns of language: which words follow which, how arguments are structured, what an email sounds like. In this lesson, you'll see how that works by training a model yourself.

cards.title: It predicts, it doesn't look up
cards.body: An LLM has no built-in fact database. It generates text that sounds right, one likely token at a time.

cards.title: Gaps in its training data
cards.body: When it knows little about a topic, or the event happened after its knowledge cutoff, it fills the gap with plausible guesses.

cards.title: Built to sound helpful
cards.body: It's trained to give fluent, confident answers. Sounding sure is not the same as being right.

columns.title: AI is good at
columns.body:
- Spotting patterns in huge amounts of data
- Predicting what's likely to happen next
- Generating text, images and code quickly
- Translating and summarising
- Working at a speed and scale no human can
- Doing the same task consistently, without tiring

columns.title: AI struggles with
columns.body:
- Guaranteeing that what it says is true
- Knowing about events after it was trained
- Common sense in unfamiliar situations
- Understanding meaning the way people do
- Being free of bias, since it learns from human data
- Taking responsibility for decisions

data.caption: Strengths and limits of today's AI

data.prompt: Responsible AI isn't about being scared of AI. It's about knowing where it can go wrong, and having a move ready for each. Tap each risk.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Confident answers that are wrong: invented facts, fake sources, made-up quotes.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Match checking to the stakes, and run important outputs around the Verification Wheel.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Stereotypes in text and images, unfair assumptions about gender, age, religion or nationality, and one-sided answers.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Ask "who could this exclude?" Request balanced perspectives, and review anything that affects people.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Pasting personal data (names, numbers, health, money) into tools that may store it.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Use the Data Traffic Light. Replace details with placeholders, and check your tool's data settings.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Convincing AI-written phishing, fake AI apps and browser extensions, and company secrets leaking through AI tools.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Use trusted, approved tools only. Never share passwords or codes, and verify unexpected requests.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Copying others' work through AI, or using AI images or text commercially without checking the terms.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Don't paste paid content to reproduce it, credit sources, and check your tool's terms before commercial use.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Cloned voices, fake videos of real people, and fake "breaking news" images spreading on WhatsApp.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Pause before you share or pay. Verify through a trusted source or a different channel.

boxes.label: What it looks like
boxes.text: Letting AI make decisions it shouldn't, losing your own skills, or submitting AI work you don't understand.

boxes.label: Your move
boxes.text: Keep a human in charge of important decisions, understand what you submit, and disclose AI use when required.

data.prompt: AI doesn't replace jobs in one go. It changes individual tasks. Pick a job and sort each of its tasks: will AI mostly **automate** it, **assist** a person with it, or will it stay **mostly human**? Then compare with an expert view.

scenarios.label: Marketing executive

items.why: Repetitive and rule-based. Tools already do it.

items.text: Write first drafts of social posts
items.why: AI drafts quickly; you add brand voice, real details and judgement.
AI finds patterns fast; you decide what they mean and what to do.
Scheduling tools and automations handle it.
AI can offer ideas, but strategy needs judgement and accountability.

items.text: Build relationships with clients and partners
items.why: Trust is built person to person.

scenarios.closing: The marketing executive doesn't disappear. The job shifts towards the human tasks, with AI handling or speeding up the rest.

scenarios.label: Teacher

items.why: Fully rule-based, and easy to check.
AI drafts questions; you check accuracy and level.
AI suggests activities and resources; you shape them for your class.
AI can suggest comments; the teacher decides the grade and tone.
Simple data entry, easily automated.
Care, trust and knowing the child are human.

scenarios.closing: The teacher doesn't disappear. The job shifts towards the human tasks, with AI handling or speeding up the rest.

scenarios.label: Accountant

items.text: Enter invoice data into the system
items.why: AI can read invoices and fill fields, with exceptions checked.
Matching transactions is rule-based and increasingly automated.
AI flags patterns; an accountant investigates.
AI drafts; the accountant verifies every figure.

items.text: Advise a client on tax planning
items.why: Regulated, high-stakes advice needs a qualified, accountable person.

items.text: Explain results to a nervous business owner
items.why: Clear, empathetic explanation builds trust.

scenarios.closing: The accountant doesn't disappear. The job shifts towards the human tasks, with AI handling or speeding up the rest.

scenarios.label: Customer support agent

items.why: Classification is an AI strength, as you saw in Lesson 19.
An assistant grounded in the FAQ can handle these, with spot-checks.
AI drafts; the agent checks facts and tone.
AI summarises; the agent confirms nothing important is missing.

items.text: Calm an angry customer on the phone
items.why: Empathy and real-time judgement stay human.
Money and fairness decisions need human accountability.

scenarios.closing: The customer support agent doesn't disappear. The job shifts towards the human tasks, with AI handling or speeding up the rest.

data.footnote: These are informed judgements about likely change over the next few years, not predictions. Different workplaces will adopt AI at very different speeds.

sentences.text: Dear Principals, we're excited to invite your students to the Karachi Youth Tech Summit 2026!
The summit takes place on Sunday 14 November at the Expo Centre, Hall 2.
sentences.why: The brief says Saturday, not Sunday.
sentences.fix: The summit takes place on Saturday 14 November, 9:30am–5pm, at the Expo Centre, Hall 2.

sentences.text: Karachi is Pakistan's largest city and a major port on the Arabian Sea.
sentences.why: True, but irrelevant. Principals don't need a geography lesson.

sentences.text: It's a free event, so there's no limit on how many students can attend.
sentences.why: Free doesn't mean unlimited: there are only 200 seats, first come first served.
sentences.fix: The event is free, but places are limited to 200 students, first come first served.

sentences.text: The day will feature 10 confirmed speakers from leading tech companies.
sentences.why: The brief says 6 confirmed speakers, and doesn't say where they're from.
sentences.fix: The day will feature 6 confirmed speakers.

sentences.text: According to a 2024 UNESCO report, 90% of students who attend tech summits find jobs within a year.
sentences.why: This statistic isn't in the brief, and there's no evidence the report exists. It's very likely invented.
sentences.fix: (Delete this sentence, unless you can find and cite the real source.)

sentences.text: The summit is ideal for boys aged 16–24 who are interested in engineering.
sentences.why: The brief says all genders are welcome. This excludes girls, and narrows it to engineering.
sentences.fix: The summit is open to all students aged 16–24 who are curious about technology.

sentences.text: Lunch is provided, and students should bring their student ID.
For any questions, call our venue manager Imran directly on 0300-1234567.
sentences.why: This shares a private, internal-only phone number. That's a privacy breach.

sentences.text: We look forward to seeing your students there!

data.prompt: Think of a problem from your study, work or home. Answer five honest questions about it, and the decision tree will tell you what to do. Try it with two different problems.

questions.text: Is this task repeated often, or does it involve a lot of information?
questions.hint: One-off tasks are often quicker to just do yourself.

questions.text: Would a simpler fix work: a checklist, a template, a reminder, or a conversation?
questions.hint: Be honest. Simple fixes are cheaper, faster and safer.

questions.text: Does it involve text, images, data or patterns: writing, summarising, sorting, answering, analysing?
questions.hint: These are the things AI is good at.

questions.text: If AI gets it wrong, can a person catch and fix the mistake before it causes harm?
questions.hint: Think about health, money, safety and people's rights.

questions.text: Does it need sensitive personal data: health, finances, ID numbers, private details?

outcomes.title: Probably not worth it
outcomes.body: For a one-off task, setting up AI may take longer than doing it yourself. You can still use a chat assistant for a quick first draft or idea.

outcomes.title: Try the simple fix first
outcomes.body: Start with the non-AI fix. If the problem is still there after a few weeks, come back and consider AI.

outcomes.title: Not an AI problem
outcomes.body: This sounds like a physical, technical or people problem. AI might help you research solutions, but it won't solve it directly.

outcomes.title: High risk: keep humans in charge
outcomes.body: Use AI only as an assistant that suggests, with a qualified person making every decision, or don't use AI here at all.

outcomes.title: Possible, with strong safeguards
outcomes.body: Only use approved tools, remove or replace personal details, and keep a human reviewing every output. Check your organisation's policy first.

outcomes.title: A good AI opportunity
outcomes.body: Start small, measure the before and after, and keep a person reviewing the outputs. This could make a great capstone.
